expertInsight: This exam is hard because it covers so many ways to connect systems: REST, SOAP, Bulk API, Platform Events, Change Data Capture, outbound messages, MuleSoft and Heroku Connect. The questions that slowed me down were the ones where the scenario was vague about timing. If the question doesn't say the user needs an answer right away, it usually isn't asking for a synchronous callout. Know the callout limits by heart (100 callouts per transaction, 120 seconds total). Also know what happens when a trigger hands work off to @future or Queueable. I got more questions on Connected Apps, OAuth and Canvas than I expected, so don't skip them.

whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Integration Architect exam for?

personas.label: Senior developers
personas.description: You already build callouts and APIs, and you want proof that you can design the whole integration, not just code one part of it.

personas.label: Aspiring architects
personas.description: Platform Integration Architect is one of the four exams you need for System Architect, which in turn leads toward Technical Architect (CTA).

personas.label: Integration consultants
personas.description: You connect Salesforce to ERPs, billing tools and data platforms for clients, and you want a credential that shows it.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Integration Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: Yes. Most people rate it as one of the harder architect exams. You need to know the Salesforce APIs well, and you also need to know when not to use them and reach for middleware instead.
bullets: 67% to pass. That is about 41 correct answers out of 60. Most questions are scenarios, so you can't pass on memory alone.
Many patterns tested. Expect REST, SOAP, Bulk API, Platform Events, Change Data Capture, outbound messages and MuleSoft.
Limits matter. Callout limits (100 per transaction, 120 seconds total) and async Apex come up often.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: People with a few years of real integration work tend to do best. Before you book, aim for 75% or more on practice tests, and make sure you can sketch an integration on a whiteboard and explain why you chose each piece.

examFormat.heading: Integration Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: About two thirds of the questions are short business scenarios. A typical one describes data that needs to move between Salesforce and another system, then asks which approach fits best: real time, near real time or batch, and push or pull.
bestWayToPass: Learn the patterns first: For each scenario, ask three things. Does the user wait for an answer? How much data is there? Which system starts the exchange? Those answers point to the pattern.
Know the callout limits: 100 callouts per transaction and 120 seconds in total. Know when to move work into @future or Queueable Apex to stay under them.
Don't skip Connected Apps: Know the main OAuth flows, what scopes do, and how Canvas apps load an outside app inside Salesforce.
Know when to add middleware: A single, simple connection can go direct. Many systems, heavy data changes or reuse across teams usually means MuleSoft or another middleware tool.

introLead.text: Platform Integration Architect checks that you can design how Salesforce connects to other systems, from start to finish. It is one of the four exams you need for System Architect. See the

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you design connections between Salesforce and other systems using the REST, SOAP, Bulk and streaming APIs. You pick the right pattern, decide whether middleware is needed, and plan what happens when something fails.

blocks.heading: Integration Patterns: When to Use Each
blocks.body: Salesforce publishes a short list of integration patterns, and most exam questions map to one of them. **Request and Reply:** Salesforce calls another system and waits for the answer, for example checking an address while a user saves a record. **Fire and Forget:** Salesforce sends a message and moves on without waiting. Platform Events and outbound messages work this way. **Batch Data Synchronization:** large amounts of data move on a schedule, usually with Bulk API or an ETL tool such as MuleSoft or Informatica. **Data Virtualization:** Salesforce shows outside data without storing it, using External Objects and Salesforce Connect. **UI Update Based on Data Changes:** Change Data Capture or the streaming API pushes changes to a screen as they happen. To pick the right one, look at three things in the question: how fast the answer is needed, how much data there is, and what should happen if the call fails.

blocks.heading: Salesforce APIs: REST, SOAP, Bulk, Streaming, and Connect
blocks.body: Each API fits a different job. **REST API** uses JSON and is the default for small, real-time reads and writes, both into Salesforce and out through Apex callouts. **SOAP API** uses XML and a WSDL, and you mostly see it with older enterprise systems that want a strict contract. **Bulk API 2.0** handles millions of records in the background and is the usual choice for data migration and large nightly loads. **Change Data Capture** sends an event every time a record changes, with only the fields that changed. **Composite API** groups several REST calls into one request, which saves round trips. **Connect API** gives ready-made endpoints for things like Chatter and Experience Cloud. The exam asks which API fits a given amount of data, speed and direction, and which limits apply. Remember 100 callouts per transaction, a 6 MB heap limit for synchronous Apex and the daily API call allowance for your org.

blocks.heading: Error Handling, Idempotency, and Recovery
blocks.body: Integrations fail, and the exam wants to see that you planned for it. **Retry with backoff:** wait a little longer before each retry (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s) so you don't flood a system that is already struggling. **Idempotency:** sending the same message twice should not create two records. The usual fix is an external ID or a unique request ID that the receiving system checks. **Dead-letter queue:** messages that still fail after every retry go to a holding area where someone can look at them. **Circuit breaker:** after several failures in a row, stop calling the other system for a while and queue the work instead. Two Salesforce details come up often. Outbound messages are retried for up to 24 hours. Platform Event subscribers can use the replay ID to pick up where they left off, and events are kept for 72 hours.

blocks.heading: Platform Events, CDC, and Event-Driven Architecture
blocks.body: **Platform Events** let one system announce that something happened while other systems listen. Apex, Flow or an outside system can publish an event. Apex triggers, Flow or outside subscribers can react to it. The publisher doesn't need to know who is listening, which is why this is called loose coupling. Events are kept for 72 hours, and each one has a replay ID so a subscriber that went offline can catch up. **Change Data Capture (CDC)** is a special kind of event that Salesforce sends for you whenever a record is created, updated, deleted or undeleted. Each CDC event tells you what changed, the type of change and who made it. Outside systems can subscribe with CometD or with the newer Pub/Sub API, which uses gRPC and is the better choice for new work. On the exam, use Platform Events when you control the message, CDC when you just need to mirror record changes, and outbound messages for simple, no-code notifications.

blocks.heading: Middleware, MuleSoft, and API Governance
blocks.body: Once more than two or three systems are involved, connecting each one directly to the others turns into a mess. Middleware sits in the middle and handles the routing and data mapping. MuleSoft splits APIs into three layers. **System APIs** talk to the back-end systems. **Process APIs** combine data and apply business rules. **Experience APIs** shape the data for a specific app or channel. Anypoint Exchange is where teams publish APIs so others can reuse them, and an API gateway enforces rate limits and security. On the Salesforce side, **Named Credentials** hold the endpoint URL and the login details, so your Apex code never contains a password or token. When a question shows hard-coded auth headers, the answer is almost always Named Credentials. **External Services** let an admin import an OpenAPI spec and call that API from Flow with no code. Expect questions on when middleware is worth the cost and how to retire an old API version without breaking the systems that use it.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Integration Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Almost every question is a design choice. Read the scenario, find the details about timing, volume and failure, and let those pick the answer for you.

blocks.heading: Integration Pattern Selection
blocks.body: If the user is waiting on screen, think Request and Reply. If nobody is waiting, think Fire and Forget or batch. If the data shouldn't be copied into Salesforce at all, think Data Virtualization.

blocks.heading: REST vs. SOAP vs. Bulk API
blocks.body: **REST API** for small, quick reads and writes. **SOAP API** when the other system needs a WSDL. **Bulk API** once you are into tens of thousands of records or more. Streaming and CDC when the other side needs to hear about changes as they happen.

blocks.heading: Platform Events & Change Data Capture
blocks.body: **Platform Events** when you design the message yourself and want publisher and subscriber kept apart. **CDC** when you just need to copy record changes somewhere else. In both cases, know how the replay ID lets a subscriber catch up after it was offline.

blocks.heading: Middleware & MuleSoft
blocks.body: One simple connection can go direct. Several systems, a lot of data mapping, or APIs that other teams will reuse point to middleware. Know the three MuleSoft layers: System, Process and Experience.

blocks.heading: Security in Integrations
blocks.body: Use **Named Credentials** for every outbound call. Pick the **OAuth** flow that fits: JWT bearer for server-to-server, web server flow when a person logs in. Add IP restrictions or mutual TLS when the data is sensitive.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After Integration Architect, most people work toward System Architect and then CTA:

sampleQuestions.question: When a sales rep saves an Account, the address must be checked by an outside address service. The rep should see an error straight away if the address is wrong. Which pattern fits best?
options: Fire and Forget using a Platform Event
Batch Data Synchronization running every night
Request and Reply using a synchronous callout
Data Virtualization using External Objects
sampleQuestions.explanation: The rep is waiting and needs the result before the save finishes. That is Request and Reply: Salesforce calls the service and waits for the answer.
whyWrong: A Platform Event doesn't wait for a reply, so the rep wouldn't see the error while saving.
A nightly batch runs hours later. The rep would already have moved on.
External Objects show outside data inside Salesforce. They don't check data the user is typing in.

sampleQuestions.question: A company needs to load 8 million order records from an old ERP into Salesforce during a one-time migration. Which API should the architect recommend?
options: Bulk API 2.0
REST API with one call per record
Composite API
SOAP API with synchronous calls
sampleQuestions.explanation: Bulk API 2.0 is built for very large loads. It processes records in the background in large chunks and uses far fewer API calls.
whyWrong: One REST call per record would use 8 million API calls and blow through the org's daily limit.
Composite API groups a few requests together, but it is meant for small related changes, not millions of rows.
Synchronous SOAP calls have the same volume problem as REST and would be very slow.

sampleQuestions.question: A developer has written an Apex callout with the API username and password typed into the code as an Authorization header. What should the architect recommend instead?
options: Store the password in a Custom Setting and read it in the code
Use a Named Credential to hold the endpoint and authentication
Encrypt the password and keep it in a Custom Label
Ask the other system to drop authentication for Salesforce IP addresses
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Named Credential keeps the URL and login details out of the code. Salesforce adds the authentication for you, and admins can change it without a deployment.
whyWrong: A Custom Setting is still readable by admins and code, and you still have to build the auth header by hand.
Custom Labels are not meant for secrets, and anyone with setup access can read them.
Removing authentication makes the other system less secure. IP checks can be added on top of login, not used instead of it.

sampleQuestions.question: Every time an Opportunity is updated, a data warehouse needs a copy of only the fields that changed. The team does not want to write custom code to send these changes. What is the best fit?
options: An Apex trigger that makes a REST callout on each update
A scheduled report emailed to the warehouse team
A custom Platform Event published from Flow
Change Data Capture on the Opportunity object
sampleQuestions.explanation: Change Data Capture sends an event for each change automatically, and the event holds only the changed fields. The warehouse just subscribes.
whyWrong: A trigger with callouts is custom code, and it can hit callout limits during bulk updates.
A scheduled report is not a real integration and doesn't capture each individual change.
A custom Platform Event works, but you would have to build and publish it yourself. CDC does this for you.

sampleQuestions.question: An external billing system sometimes sends the same invoice message twice after a network timeout. Duplicate invoices are being created in Salesforce. What should the architect do?
options: Turn off retries in the billing system
Upsert using an external ID taken from the invoice number
Add a nightly job that finds and deletes the duplicate invoices
Increase the API timeout to 10 minutes
sampleQuestions.explanation: An upsert on an external ID updates the record if it already exists, so a repeated message doesn't create a second invoice. This makes the integration idempotent.
whyWrong: Turning off retries means real failures are never recovered.
A cleanup job leaves duplicates in place for hours and fixes the symptom, not the cause.
A longer timeout might reduce retries, but it won't stop them. Duplicates can still happen.

sampleQuestions.question: An external subscriber to Salesforce Platform Events was offline for 6 hours during maintenance. How can it get the events it missed?
options: It can't. Events are lost if no one is listening
Ask Salesforce support to resend them
Rebuild all of the missed data using a full nightly export
Reconnect using the replay ID of the last event it processed
sampleQuestions.explanation: Platform Events are kept for 72 hours. A subscriber can pass the last replay ID it handled and receive everything published after that point.
whyWrong: Events are not lost straight away. They are kept for 72 hours so subscribers can catch up.
Support doesn't resend events. The replay ID is the built-in way to do this.
A full export is slow and unnecessary when the events are still available to replay.

sampleQuestions.question: A company is connecting Salesforce to an ERP, a warehouse system, a billing tool and a customer portal. Several teams will reuse the same customer and order data. What should the architect recommend?
options: Middleware with reusable APIs
Direct point-to-point connections between every pair of systems
Nightly CSV files on a shared FTP server
Let each team build its own Apex callouts
sampleQuestions.explanation: With many systems and shared data, middleware keeps the connections in one place. Reusable System and Process APIs stop each team rebuilding the same thing.
whyWrong: Point-to-point links grow quickly with each new system and become hard to change.
Nightly files are slow, error-prone and don't give teams reusable services.
Separate callouts per team mean duplicated logic and no central place to manage security or changes.

sampleQuestions.question: A partner's server needs to call the Salesforce REST API every 15 minutes with no person logging in. Which OAuth flow fits best?
options: Web server (authorization code) flow
User-agent flow
JWT bearer flow
Username and password flow
sampleQuestions.explanation: The JWT bearer flow is meant for server-to-server access. The partner signs a token with a certificate and gets access without anyone typing a password.
whyWrong: The web server flow needs a person to log in and approve access in a browser.
The user-agent flow is for apps running in a browser or on a device, with a user present.
The username and password flow stores a real password on the server and is not recommended.

sampleQuestions.question: A trigger starts one Queueable job that makes a callout for every record in the transaction. During a data load, a single transaction can include 500 records. What is the main risk?
options: The trigger will run twice for each record
The transaction will hit the limit of 100 callouts
Callouts from triggers are always blocked by Salesforce
The records will be saved without an ID
sampleQuestions.explanation: Apex allows 100 callouts per transaction, and the Queueable job runs as one transaction. 500 callouts would fail. Group the records into fewer calls or split the work across several jobs or batch Apex.
whyWrong: Triggers can re-run in some cases, but that is not the main risk in this scenario.
Callouts from a Queueable job started by a trigger are allowed. That is the usual way to call out after a record change.
Records get IDs when they are inserted. Callouts don't affect that.

sampleQuestions.question: Service agents need to see a customer's recent shipments, which live in a logistics system. The data changes constantly and must not be copied into Salesforce. Which approach fits?
options: Copy the shipments into a custom object every hour
Send shipment updates by outbound message
Load shipment history with Bulk API each night
Salesforce Connect with External Objects
sampleQuestions.explanation: Salesforce Connect reads the data from the logistics system when the agent opens the page. Nothing is stored in Salesforce, and the data is always current.
whyWrong: An hourly copy stores the data in Salesforce, which the scenario rules out, and it can be an hour out of date.
Outbound messages send data out of Salesforce. They don't bring outside data in.
A nightly Bulk load copies the data and is up to a day old.

sampleQuestions.question: An admin wants to call an outside currency rate API from a Flow without writing any Apex. The API has an OpenAPI spec. What should they use?
options: External Services
Outbound messages
A Canvas app
Change Data Capture
sampleQuestions.explanation: External Services reads the OpenAPI spec and creates actions that Flow can call directly. No code is needed.
whyWrong: Outbound messages send a fixed SOAP message out of Salesforce. They can't read a response back into a Flow.
A Canvas app shows an outside web app inside Salesforce. It doesn't give Flow a callable action.
CDC publishes changes to Salesforce records. It doesn't call outside APIs.

sampleQuestions.question: When a Case is closed, a ticket must be closed in an outside help desk tool. The user doesn't need to wait for this, and the team wants a declarative option with built-in retries. What fits?
options: A synchronous Apex callout in a before-update trigger
A nightly batch job
An outbound message from a record-triggered Flow
A Lightning component that calls the help desk from the browser
sampleQuestions.explanation: Outbound messages are no-code, don't make the user wait, and Salesforce retries them for up to 24 hours if the other system is down.
whyWrong: Triggers can't make synchronous callouts, and this would make the user wait anyway.
A nightly job delays the update by up to a day for no reason.
A browser call only runs when someone has the page open, and it puts the integration logic on the user's screen.

sampleQuestions.question: An outside order system is having an outage, and every call to it times out after 10 seconds. Salesforce keeps calling it and users are stuck waiting. Which design helps most?
options: Raise the timeout to 120 seconds
Retry each call right away in a loop
Remove error handling so the calls fail faster
A circuit breaker that pauses calls and queues work
sampleQuestions.explanation: A circuit breaker notices repeated failures and stops calling the broken system for a set time. Work is queued and sent once the system is back.
whyWrong: A longer timeout makes users wait even longer and doesn't fix the outage.
Instant retries add load to a system that is already down and use up callout limits.
Removing error handling means failed work is lost with no record of it.

sampleQuestions.question: Version 1 of a company's customer API is being replaced by version 2, which changes some field names. Five other systems use version 1. What is the safest plan?
options: Switch everyone to version 2 on the same day
Run both versions side by side, announce a retirement date
Change version 1 in place so it returns the new field names
Keep version 1 forever and never release version 2
sampleQuestions.explanation: Running both versions for a while gives each consumer time to update and test. A clear retirement date keeps the move on track.
whyWrong: A same-day switch means any consumer that isn't ready will break.
Changing version 1 in place breaks every system that relies on the old field names.
Never moving on leaves the team stuck maintaining old code and blocks improvements.

sampleQuestions.question: An external app needs to create an Account, a Contact and an Opportunity together. If any one fails, none should be saved. The team wants as few API calls as possible. What should they use?
options: Three separate REST API calls
Bulk API 2.0 with three jobs
Composite API with allOrNone true
Three outbound messages
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Composite API sends all three requests in one call. With allOrNone set to true, everything is rolled back if one part fails.
whyWrong: Three separate calls use more API calls, and if the third fails the first two are already saved.
Bulk API is for large volumes and runs in the background. It is far too heavy for three related records.
Outbound messages send data out of Salesforce. They can't be used by an outside app to create records.
